paper.title: Accelerating Diffusion Sampling via Speculative Draft Trees
paper.abstract: Abstract Speculative sampling accelerates diffusion model generation by drafting inexpensive candidate states and correcting them under a coupling that preserves the target distribution exactly , reducing the number of expensive target evaluations. Existing diffusion samplers, notably those based on reflection maximal coupling, are topologically constrained: their lookahead drafts form a chain graph, a single linear sequence, which inherently limits the acceptance rate per target evaluation. We connect speculative sampling in diffusion models to relative entropy coding (REC). This perspective shows the lookahead need not be linear and motivates our central contribution, draft trees , which enrich the candidates considered per round and lower the target function evaluations. We further adopt greedy rejection sampling, an REC algorithm, as the draft–target coupling, improving acceptance while guaranteeing exact target samples. Experiments across diverse target and draft models demonstrate up to 8.3% acceleration over the reflection coupling baseline in practical settings.

sections.heading: 1  Introduction
sections.text: Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021b ) have become the dominant paradigm for high-fidelity image generation. By learning to reverse a gradual noising process, diffusion models synthesize images through a sequence of denoising steps that progressively transform Gaussian noise into a sample from the target data distribution. Their remarkable generation quality has established diffusion models as the state of the art across a wide range of generative tasks ( Yang et al., 2023 ) . Figure 1 : Efficiency frontier of speculative sampling. The plot compares the maximal speedup attainable over a standard sampler at a given proposal budget B B for the setting described in Section 5.1 . By allocating budget strictly to sequential depth, RMC rapidly saturates near a 2.00 × 2.00\times speedup. In contrast, D-GRS allocates budget to multiple proposals per node, effectively raising the per-step acceptance probability. This branching strategy allows D-GRS to monotonically convert larger budgets into measurable acceleration, up to a 14 % 14\% reduction in target model evaluations relative to RMC. A major drawback of diffusion models, however, is their high inference cost. Image generation requires repeatedly evaluating a large neural network over tens to hundreds of denoising iterations, making sampling extremely slow. This computational bottleneck has motivated a broad range of acceleration techniques. Training-free approaches include improved solvers to reduce the number of sampling steps ( Zhang and Chen, 2023 ; Lu et al., 2025 ) , while training-based methods learn few-step generators, either by preserving the sampling trajectory, as in consistency models ( Song et al., 2023 ) and their two-time flow-map generalizations ( Geng et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Sabour et al., 2025 ) , recently extended to learn the solution map of the underlying SDE ( McCallum et al., 2026 ) , or by directly matching the output distribution ( Yin et al., 2024a ; Sauer et al., 2024 ) . While effective in reducing latency, these approaches typically incur either additional training cost or degradation in sample quality ( Dieleman, 2026 ; Lai et al., 2025 ) . Parallel simulation provides an orthogonal acceleration strategy, trading additional computation and memory for reduced latency ( Shih et al., 2023 ; Tang et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Zhou and Sugiyama, 2025 ) . Despite reducing the sequential depth of diffusion sampling, it typically requires multiple iterative refinement rounds and substantial parallel resources. Recently, speculative diffusion sampling ( De Bortoli et al., 2025 ) has emerged as a complementary paradigm for accelerating diffusion inference. Inspired by speculative decoding for large language models ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) , these methods first generate candidate denoising states using an inexpensive source (referred to as a proposal ) before verifying them using the target diffusion model. Whenever multiple draft states are accepted, several denoising iterations are effectively skipped, leading directly to lower inference latency. Crucially, unlike approximate acceleration techniques, speculative diffusion sampling is exact : it preserves the sampling distribution of the target model, and therefore incurs no loss in image quality. Despite these advantages, existing speculative diffusion samplers are fundamentally topology constrained . They generate drafts sequentially along the diffusion trajectory, resulting in a linear chain of proposal states. From a broader perspective, speculative sampling is a budget allocation problem: given a fixed amount of parallel computation, how should proposal evaluations be allocated to maximize the probability of accepting draft states? Restricting proposals to a chain represents only one possible allocation strategy and can leave substantial parallelism underutilized, particularly in the low-acceptance regime that commonly arises in practice. In this paper, we take a first step toward lifting this restriction. Our contributions are two-fold. First, we generalize speculative diffusion sampling from linear draft chains to draft trees , enabling substantially richer allocations of parallel computation across candidate denoising trajectories. Second, we establish a novel connection between speculative sampling and relative entropy coding (REC) ( Li, 2024 ; Li and El Gamal, 2018 ; Flamich and Theis, 2023 ; Flamich, 2023 ) . This connection leads naturally to a greedy rejection sampling (GRS) ( Harsha et al., 2010 ) strategy for budget allocation, providing an efficient and principled mechanism for constructing draft trees. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach consistently improves speculative diffusion sampling, achieving speedups of up to 7.4% over existing methods for practical batch sizes ≤ 256 \leq 256 , while preserving exact sampling (see Figure 1 ).

sections.heading: Speculative diffusion sampling.
sections.text: The principal computational bottleneck in diffusion inference is the repeated evaluation of the reverse drift b t n q b_{t_{n}}^{q} , which is parameterized by a large neural network. Since Euler–Maruyama simulation proceeds sequentially, each state Y n + 1 Y_{n+1} depends on the reverse drift evaluated at the preceding state Y n Y_{n} , limiting the utilization of modern parallel hardware. Speculative diffusion sampling addresses this bottleneck by exploiting parallel computation. Rather than simulating one denoising step at a time, an inexpensive proposal model first generates multiple draft states. The key assumption underlying speculative sampling is that drafting is significantly cheaper than verification . The drafted states are subsequently verified using the target reverse drift in parallel. Consequently, given a parallel compute budget of B B , one batched target-model evaluation, corresponding to one neural function evaluation (NFE), can verify all proposed drafts. The effectiveness of speculative sampling depends critically on the quality of the proposal model. Better proposals lead to higher acceptance rates, allowing more denoising steps to be advanced per NFE and thereby increasing the overall speedup while preserving exact sampling. Existing speculative diffusion methods ( De Bortoli et al., 2025 ) consider two proposal mechanisms. The first trains a lightweight diffusion model to approximate the target reverse drift. The second, referred to as the delayed reverse drift , avoids additional training by replacing the current reverse drift with one evaluated at an earlier state. Specifically, the target transition mean m n q ​ ( y n ) = y n + γ ​ b t n q ​ ( y n ) m_{n}^{q}(y_{n})=y_{n}+\gamma{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}b_{t_{n}}^{q}(y_{n})} is approximated by the proposal mean m n p ​ ( y n ) = y n + γ ​ b t k q ​ ( y k ) , k < n , \displaystyle m_{n}^{p}(y_{n})=y_{n}+\gamma{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}b_{t_{k}}^{q}(y_{k})},\qquad k<n\ , (7) while retaining the same transition variance σ n 2 = γ ​ ε 2 ​ g 1 − t n 2 \sigma_{n}^{2}=\gamma\varepsilon^{2}g_{1-t_{n}}^{2} . Empirically, delayed reverse drift has been shown to produce higher-quality proposals than lightweight draft models ( De Bortoli et al., 2025 ) . Accordingly, we adopt it as the proposal mechanism throughout this paper.

sections.heading: 3  Speculative Algorithms
sections.text: In this section, we first state the general template that both algorithms instantiate, then review the reflection maximal coupling (RMC) algorithm of ( De Bortoli et al., 2025 ) , and finally introduce our diffusion-GRS (D-GRS) algorithm. At a high level, every speculative sampling algorithm consists of three phases: a drafting phase, a verification phase, and an acceptance phase. Given a parallel compute budget, the drafting phase sequentially generates candidate states according to a prescribed draft topology, the verification phase evaluates all drafted states in parallel using the target model, and the acceptance phase sequentially examines the verified states to determine whether a proposal can be accepted as the next target state. Consequently, speculative sampling algorithms differ primarily in the choice of draft topology and the acceptance criterion used after verification. Both RMC and D-GRS rely on a common one-dimensional reduction that exploits the translation and rotational invariance of isotropic Gaussian distributions, described next. Throughout, we use Y ^ \widehat{Y} (or S ^ \widehat{S} ) to denote a proposed state and Y Y (or S S ) to denote the accepted target state.

sections.heading: 3.1  Round Structure
sections.text: Algorithm 1 describes the speculative diffusion sampling procedure for an arbitrary draft tree 𝒯 \mathcal{T} . Each iteration of the algorithm involves three distinct phases. 1. The drafting phase executes a layer-wise expansion of the tree: this expansion is strictly sequential with respect to depth, as child nodes cannot be sampled prior to their respective parents. However, all nodes residing at the same depth level are generated concurrently. 2. The verification phase computes the target means for all internal nodes of the current tree via a unified batched operation, representing the sole evaluation of the target model within a given iteration. 3. Finally, the acceptance phase traverses downward from the root node, iteratively applying the verification criterion at each depth level and terminating immediately upon encountering the first rejection. The verification rule, denoted as Verify , serves as a modular component within this framework and is governed by the following formal contract. Given a parent node u u , its associated proposal and target means, the corresponding step scale, and its set of drafted children { Y ^ v } v ∈ 𝒞 ⁡ ( u ) \{\widehat{Y}_{v}\}_{v\in\mathcal{C}(u)} , the rule outputs a tuple ( Y , accepted , v ⋆ ) (Y,\texttt{accepted},v^{\star}) . The primary component, Y Y , constitutes an exact sample drawn from the target transition distribution, Y ∼ ℚ ( ⋅ ∣ Y ^ u ) Y\sim\mathbb{Q}\big(\cdot\mid\widehat{Y}_{u}\big) . This sample is obtained through one of two mutually exclusive mechanisms: either a valid child node is identified, wherein the boolean flag accepted evaluates to true and Y = Y ^ v ⋆ Y=\widehat{Y}_{v^{\star}} for a specific v ⋆ ∈ 𝒞 ⁡ ( u ) v^{\star}\in\mathcal{C}(u) ; alternatively, if no child satisfies the criterion, accepted evaluates to false, and Y Y is instead sampled from the normalized residual distribution formulated in ( 17 ) below. Algorithm 3 fulfills this contract for any arbitrary branching factor K ≥ 1 K\geq 1 , whereas Algorithm 2 is specialized for K = 1 K=1 . The template leaves exactly two components free: the draft topology 𝒯 \mathcal{T} and the verification rule Verify . The remainder of this section instantiates them. RMC takes 𝒯 \mathcal{T} to be a chain ( K = 1 K=1 ) and Verify to be the reflection maximal coupling by ( De Bortoli et al., 2025 ) ; D-GRS takes 𝒯 \mathcal{T} to be a K K -ary tree and Verify to be our proposed D-GRS algorithm. sections.heading: 3.2  Reflection Maximal Coupling (RMC)
sections.text: RMC ( De Bortoli et al., 2025 ) instantiates the speculative sampling framework using a chain topology and reflection maximal coupling for acceptance. Specifically, the drafting phase sequentially generates a chain of L L proposal states, where L L is referred to as the lookahead . During the acceptance phase, each proposal is maximally coupled with the corresponding target transition, thereby minimizing the probability of rejecting the drafted state. Given a compute budget of W = 7 W=7 states, RMC constructs a single proposal chain. If an early proposal is rejected, all downstream proposals become unusable and are discarded. In contrast, D-GRS constructs a K K -ary draft tree, here with K = 2 K=2 and L = 2 L=2 . At each level, D-GRS may select among multiple candidate states, increasing the probability that at least one proposal can be accepted. Topology: The chain employed by RMC represents only one possible allocation of a fixed parallel compute budget. To exploit this budget more effectively, we introduce a more flexible topology based on draft trees , depicted in Figure 2 . A K K -ary draft tree expands every non-leaf node into K K children, each representing a candidate realization of the next target state. Suppose drafting begins at time step n n , and let Y n Y_{n} denote the current accepted target state, obtained either from the preceding draft tree or through residual sampling. We treat Y n Y_{n} as the root of the tree and draw K K conditionally independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) proposals from the proposal transition kernel at time n + 1 n+1 . Each resulting proposal is then recursively expanded into K K children, yielding a tree with L L levels, excluding the root. Conditional on a parent state, its K K children are sampled independently from this delayed-drift proposal kernel. In contrast to RMC, where each proposed state is individually coupled with the target through a maximal coupling, tree-based speculative sampling requires selecting one state from a list of proposals and coupling the selected state with the target. This naturally gives rise to a list-coupling problem. More precisely, maximal coupling minimizes the Hamming cost 𝟙 { Y ^ ≠ Y } \mathds{1}\{\widehat{Y}\neq Y\} between a single proposal Y ^ ∼ ℙ \widehat{Y}\sim\mathbb{P} and a target sample Y ∼ ℚ Y\sim\mathbb{Q} . At each node of our draft tree, however, we are given K K conditionally i.i.d. proposals Y ^ 1 , … , Y ^ K ∼ ℙ \widehat{Y}_{1},\ldots,\widehat{Y}_{K}\sim\mathbb{P} and seek a coupling that minimizes the membership cost 𝟙 { Y ∉ { Y ^ 1 , … , Y ^ K } } \mathds{1}\bigl\{Y\notin\{\widehat{Y}_{1},\ldots,\widehat{Y}_{K}\}\bigr\} . The optimal transport formulation of Sun et al. (2023) characterizes the coupling that minimizes this cost. However, computing the optimal transport plan requires solving a linear program over the target domain, whose complexity grows exponentially with the number of proposals K K . This is already costly for finite discrete state spaces and does not admit a tractable direct extension to continuous diffusion transitions. Computationally efficient approaches to list coupling have been studied in the context of language models; we provide a survey in the appendix. These methods, however, do not remain computationally tractable for continuous diffusion models. As a workaround, we draw inspiration from relative entropy coding (REC) ( Li, 2024 ; Flamich and Gündüz, 2026 ) , which is closely connected to speculative sampling, as elaborated below. REC is a class of algorithms that tackles a remote sampling problem: a sender, which has access to a target distribution ℚ \mathbb{Q} and a proposal distribution ℙ \mathbb{P} , communicates an index to a receiver, which shares ℙ \mathbb{P} , allowing the receiver to reproduce an exact sample from ℚ \mathbb{Q} . The fundamental communication cost of the index is governed, up to lower-order terms, by the relative entropy D KL ( ℚ ∥ ℙ ) D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb{Q}\|\mathbb{P}) , hence the name REC. Correspondingly, REC implementations, which can be based on Poisson processes ( Li and El Gamal, 2018 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) , dithered quantization ( Zamir and Feder, 1992 ) , or rejection sampling ( Harsha et al., 2010 ; Flamich and Theis, 2023 ; Flamich, 2023 ) , need to examine Ω ~ ( exp ( D KL ( ℚ ∥ ℙ ) ) ) \tilde{\Omega}(\exp(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb{Q}\|\mathbb{P}))) shared proposals before identifying the communicated sample. This viewpoint parallels speculative sampling: both problems seek to couple proposal samples with an exact target sample while maximizing the probability that the target can be recovered from the available proposals. While RMC optimizes the single-proposal overlap, measured by the total variation distance, REC algorithms construct exact couplings by processing an ordered sequence of proposal samples. Motivated by this connection, we replace the unrestricted list-coupling problem with an order-preserving sequence-coupling problem. In list coupling, the K K proposals may be jointly matched to the target without regard to their ordering; in sequence coupling, proposals are examined in their sampled order, and the first proposal satisfying the acceptance rule is selected. sections.text: Figure 5 illustrates the empirical speed-up over the standard target sampler as a function of K K and a constrained lookahead depth of L = 2 L=2 . As the number of proposals per node ( K K ) scales from 2 2 to 7 7 , the corresponding computational budget B B expands from 6 6 to 56 56 . Consistent with prior topological analyses, the proposed method effectively translates this expanded budget into measurable acceleration. By allocating compute toward K K , D-GRS yields a monotonically increasing speedup that peaks near 1.18 × 1.18\times at K = 6 K=6 ( B = 42 B=42 ), with an increment of 6.7 % 6.7\% relative to RMC. In contrast, RMC fails to meaningfully exploit the additional budget. Bottlenecked by the geometric decay of its sequential acceptance, the reflection sampler exhibits severe saturation, plateauing between 1.10 × 1.10\times and 1.12 × 1.12\times across the entire parameter sweep. This widening performance gap clearly demonstrates that scaling multiple proposals per node ( K K ) successfully improves per-step acceptance rates, allowing the branching topology to strictly dominate the linear chain in high-dimensional text-to-image synthesis. To empirically show the exactness of both sampling procedures, we report in Table 1 the CLIP scores ( Radford et al., 2021 ) for each budget configuration, computed using openai/clip-vit-large-patch14 .

sections.heading: 6  Conclusions and Future Work
sections.text: We identify a key topological limitation of reflection maximal coupling (RMC), which allocates its speculative budget to a single draft chain. To better utilize parallel computation, we introduce draft trees and propose D-GRS, which adapts greedy rejection sampling from the relative entropy coding literature to the resulting list-coupling problem. Across our experiments, D-GRS improves NFE speed-up over RMC by up to 8.3 % 8.3\% in practical settings. This work is a first step toward more efficient speculative diffusion sampling. Important open directions include overcoming the rapid degradation of exact coupling efficiency with generation dimension and adapting the draft topology online to the proposal quality and available compute budget.

sections.heading: A.1  Diffusion Models
sections.text: Diffusion models implicitly learn data distributions from empirical samples. The generative process is initialized with a sample from a tractable prior, typically a Gaussian distribution, and iteratively denoises it to recover a sample from the target data distribution ( Lai et al., 2025 ) . This mechanism is formalized by defining a fixed forward process that progressively corrupts the data with noise, coupled with a parameterized neural network trained to reverse this corruption. Several theoretical frameworks formulate this concept, including the Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ) and noise-conditioned score networks ( Song and Ermon, 2019 ) . These were subsequently unified as discretizations of a single continuous-time stochastic differential equation (SDE) ( Song et al., 2021b ) , alongside the more recent flow matching paradigm ( Lipman et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) . Fundamentally, these formulations are mathematically equivalent up to a transformation of the model’s output parameterization and noise schedule ( Kingma et al., 2021 ; Lai et al., 2025 ) . A critical practical consequence of this equivalence is that the training objective does not uniquely dictate the sampling algorithm: models trained via denoising can be sampled deterministically using a probability flow ordinary differential equation (ODE) ( Song et al., 2021b ) , while models trained under a flow matching objective can employ stochastic sampling schemes ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2025a ) . These generative frameworks have established state-of-the-art performance across a diverse array of modalities, encompassing image synthesis ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Karras et al., 2022 ) , video generation ( Ho et al., 2022 ; Bar-Tal et al., 2024 ) , protein design ( Watson et al., 2023 ) , prediction of biomolecular structure ( Abramson et al., 2024 ) , and numerous other applications ( Yang et al., 2023 ) . Despite their empirical success, a primary limitation of diffusion models is the iterative nature of the sampling process. Efforts to accelerate inference by reducing the number of integration steps have been extensively investigated and generally branch into training-free and training-based methodologies ( Dieleman, 2024 ; Dieleman, 2026 ; Lai et al., 2025 ) . Training-free approaches leverage the fixed, pre-trained model and achieve acceleration through the deployment of advanced ODE and SDE solvers that allow for larger step sizes without compromising accuracy ( Song et al., 2021a ; Zhang and Chen, 2023 ; Lu et al., 2022 ; Lu et al., 2025 ) . Conversely, training-based methods explicitly optimize a model to execute large synthesis steps. These approaches vary along two primary axes. The first is the source of supervision: they may distill knowledge from a pretrained teacher model ( Luhman and Luhman, 2021 ; Salimans and Ho, 2022 ; Song et al., 2023 ; Sabour et al., 2025 ) or train a few-step model entirely from scratch ( Song et al., 2023 ; Frans et al., 2025 ; Geng et al., 2025 ; Boffi et al., 2025a ) . The second axis concerns the matching objective: certain techniques enforce the preservation of trajectories connecting noise to data ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ; Song et al., 2023 ; Boffi et al., 2025b ) , whereas others constrain the final model output to match the target marginal distribution ( Yin et al., 2024b ; Yin et al., 2024a ; Sauer et al., 2024 ) . While initially developed for ODE trajectories, these acceleration techniques have recently been generalized to SDEs. This includes methods that learn transition kernels to replicate the process’s marginal distributions ( Potaptchik et al., 2026 ; Holderrieth et al., 2026 ) , as well as those that learn the solution map pathwise, conditioned on specific realizations of the driving noise ( McCallum et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: A.2  Speculative Sampling for Language Models
sections.text: Standard autoregressive decoding approaches, such as top- k k sampling ( Radford et al., 2019 ; Fan et al., 2018 ) , nucleus sampling ( Holtzman et al., 2020 ) , and the permute-and-flip decoder ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) , generate tokens one at a time and therefore incur the inherent latency of one target-model call for each token. Speculative sampling ( Chen et al., 2023 ; Leviathan et al., 2023 ) alleviates this bottleneck by employing a smaller draft model to propose multiple future tokens, while the larger target model verifies these proposed continuations in parallel, with a rejection-correction step ensuring that the exact target-model distribution is preserved. The resulting efficiency gain depends on how closely the draft distribution approximates the target distribution: more accurate proposals yield higher acceptance rates and longer verified blocks. Recent works have further advanced this paradigm through optimal-transport-based token selection ( Sun et al., 2023 ) , tree-based inference and verification ( Miao et al., 2024 ) , and multi-draft architectures ( Khisti et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2025b ; Lin et al., 2026 ) . Multi-draft speculative decoding can be viewed as an application of list-coupling schemes ( Rowan et al., 2025 ) , which strictly extend ordinary coupling for speculative decoding ( Daliri et al., 2025 ) . Recently, speculative sampling has been used to accelerating the diffusion modesl ( De Bortoli et al., 2025 ; Soen et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: A.3  Relative Entropy Coding
sections.text: The sequential coupling methodology introduced here for speculative diffusion is theoretically grounded in greedy rejection sampling ( Harsha et al., 2010 ) . This technique falls within a broader family of remote coupling methods identified by various terms in the literature, including channel simulation ( Li, 2024 ) , channel synthesis ( Cuff, 2013 ) , and reverse channel coding ( Bennett et al., 2002 ) . Hereafter, we refer to this class of schemes as relative entropy coding (REC) ( Flamich and Gündüz, 2026 ) . Fundamentally, REC is formulated as a lossy compression problem designed to establish the minimal communication overhead required to simulate a target stochastic channel over a noiseless link. The nomenclature derives from the theoretical result that, in the regime of exact simulation, the fundamental lower bound on this communication cost is governed by a relative entropy measure. In this work, we employ greedy rejection sampling ( Harsha et al., 2010 ) , a methodology whose capabilities have been significantly expanded in recent literature ( Flamich and Theis, 2023 ; Flamich, 2023 ; Hill et al., 2026 ) . A parallel and prominent class of REC frameworks relies on Poisson processes. Rooted in the Poisson functional representation ( Li and El Gamal, 2018 ) -a concept intimately connected to A ∗ \mathrm{A}^{*} sampling ( Maddison et al., 2014 ; Maddison, 2016 ) -these schemes have found broad application across diverse domains. Notable examples include hypothesis testing ( Guo et al., 2024 ) , network information theory ( Li and Anantharam, 2021 ; Liu and Li, 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) , and machine learning ( He et al., 2024 ) . Related methodologies for approximate channel simulation have been proposed by Block and Polyanskiy (2023) ; Kobus et al. (2024) ; Flamich and Wells (2024) . Nevertheless, since these approaches yield inexact simulations and therefore fall short of the theoretical relative entropy limit, they are precluded from the standard definition of REC.

Existing diffusion samplers, notably those based on reflection maximal coupling, are topologically constrained: their lookahead drafts form a chain graph, a single linear sequence, which inherently limits the acceptance rate per target evaluation. We connect speculative sampling in diffusion models to relative entropy coding (REC). This perspective shows the lookahead need not be linear and motivates our central contribution, draft trees , which enrich the candidates considered per round and lower the target function evaluations. We further adopt greedy rejection sampling, an REC algorithm, as the draft–target coupling, improving acceptance while guaranteeing exact target samples. Experiments across diverse target and draft models demonstrate up to 8.3% acceleration over the reflection coupling baseline in practical settings. https://github.com/marcellobullo/tree-specdiff 1 Introduction Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021b ) have become the dominant paradigm for high-fidelity image generation. By learning to reverse a gradual noising process, diffusion models synthesize images through a sequence of denoising steps that progressively transform Gaussian noise into a sample from the target data distribution. Their remarkable generation quality has established diffusion models as the state of the art across a wide range of generative tasks ( Yang et al., 2023 ) . Figure 1 : Efficiency frontier of speculative sampling. The plot compares the maximal speedup attainable over a standard sampler at a given proposal budget B B for the setting described in Section 5.1 . By allocating budget strictly to sequential depth, RMC rapidly saturates near a 2.00 × 2.00\times speedup. In contrast, D-GRS allocates budget to multiple proposals per node, effectively raising the per-step acceptance probability. This branching strategy allows D-GRS to monotonically convert larger budgets into measurable acceleration, up to a 14 % 14\% reduction in target model evaluations relative to RMC. A major drawback of diffusion models, however, is their high inference cost. Image generation requires repeatedly evaluating a large neural network over tens to hundreds of denoising iterations, making sampling extremely slow. This computational bottleneck has motivated a broad range of acceleration techniques. Training-free approaches include improved solvers to reduce the number of sampling steps ( Zhang and Chen, 2023 ; Lu et al., 2025 ) , while training-based methods learn few-step generators, either by preserving the sampling trajectory, as in consistency models ( Song et al., 2023 ) and their two-time flow-map generalizations ( Geng et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Sabour et al., 2025 ) , recently extended to learn the solution map of the underlying SDE ( McCallum et al., 2026 ) , or by directly matching the output distribution ( Yin et al., 2024a ; Sauer et al., 2024 ) . While effective in reducing latency, these approaches typically incur either additional training cost or degradation in sample quality ( Dieleman, 2026 ; Lai et al., 2025 ) . Parallel simulation provides an orthogonal acceleration strategy, trading additional computation and memory for reduced latency ( Shih et al., 2023 ; Tang et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Zhou and Sugiyama, 2025 ) . Despite reducing the sequential depth of diffusion sampling, it typically requires multiple iterative refinement rounds and substantial parallel resources. Recently, speculative diffusion sampling ( De Bortoli et al., 2025 ) has emerged as a complementary paradigm for accelerating diffusion inference. Inspired by speculative decoding for large language models ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) , these methods first generate candidate denoising states using an inexpensive source (referred to as a proposal ) before verifying them using the target diffusion model. Whenever multiple draft states are accepted, several denoising iterations are effectively skipped, leading directly to lower inference latency. Crucially, unlike approximate acceleration techniques, speculative diffusion sampling is exact : it preserves the sampling distribution of the target model, and therefore incurs no loss in image quality. Despite these advantages, existing speculative diffusion samplers are fundamentally topology constrained . They generate drafts sequentially along the diffusion trajectory, resulting in a linear chain of proposal states. From a broader perspective, speculative sampling is a budget allocation problem: given a fixed amount of parallel computation, how should proposal evaluations be allocated to maximize the probability of accepting draft states? Restricting proposals to a chain represents only one possible allocation strategy and can leave substantial parallelism underutilized, particularly in the low-acceptance regime that commonly arises in practice. In this paper, we take a first step toward lifting this restriction. Our contributions are two-fold. First, we generalize speculative diffusion sampling from linear draft chains to draft trees , enabling substantially richer allocations of parallel computation across candidate denoising trajectories. Second, we establish a novel connection between speculative sampling and relative entropy coding (REC) ( Li, 2024 ; Li and El Gamal, 2018 ; Flamich and Theis, 2023 ; Flamich, 2023 ) . This connection leads naturally to a greedy rejection sampling (GRS) ( Harsha et al., 2010 ) strategy for budget allocation, providing an efficient and principled mechanism for constructing draft trees. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach consistently improves speculative diffusion sampling, achieving speedups of up to 7.4% over existing methods for practical batch sizes ≤ 256 \leq 256 , while preserving exact sampling (see Figure 1 ). 2 Problem Setting DDPM. Speculative diffusion sampling. The principal computational bottleneck in diffusion inference is the repeated evaluation of the reverse drift b t n q b_{t_{n}}^{q} , which is parameterized by a large neural network. Since Euler–Maruyama simulation proceeds sequentially, each state Y n + 1 Y_{n+1} depends on the reverse drift evaluated at the preceding state Y n Y_{n} , limiting the utilization of modern parallel hardware. Speculative diffusion sampling addresses this bottleneck by exploiting parallel computation. Rather than simulating one denoising step at a time, an inexpensive proposal model first generates multiple draft states. The key assumption underlying speculative sampling is that drafting is significantly cheaper than verification . The drafted states are subsequently verified using the target reverse drift in parallel. Consequently, given a parallel compute budget of B B , one batched target-model evaluation, corresponding to one neural function evaluation (NFE), can verify all proposed drafts. The effectiveness of speculative sampling depends critically on the quality of the proposal model. Better proposals lead to higher acceptance rates, allowing more denoising steps to be advanced per NFE and thereby increasing the overall speedup while preserving exact sampling. Existing speculative diffusion methods ( De Bortoli et al., 2025 ) consider two proposal mechanisms. The first trains a lightweight diffusion model to approximate the target reverse drift. The second, referred to as the delayed reverse drift , avoids additional training by replacing the current reverse drift with one evaluated at an earlier state. At a high level, every speculative sampling algorithm consists of three phases: a drafting phase, a verification phase, and an acceptance phase. Given a parallel compute budget, the drafting phase sequentially generates candidate states according to a prescribed draft topology, the verification phase evaluates all drafted states in parallel using the target model, and the acceptance phase sequentially examines the verified states to determine whether a proposal can be accepted as the next target state. In contrast to RMC, where each proposed state is individually coupled with the target through a maximal coupling, tree-based speculative sampling requires selecting one state from a list of proposals and coupling the selected state with the target. This naturally gives rise to a list-coupling problem. More precisely, maximal coupling minimizes the Hamming cost 𝟙 { Y ^ ≠ Y } \mathds{1}\{\widehat{Y}\neq Y\} between a single proposal Y ^ ∼ ℙ \widehat{Y}\sim\mathbb{P} and a target sample Y ∼ ℚ Y\sim\mathbb{Q} . The optimal transport formulation of Sun et al. (2023) characterizes the coupling that minimizes this cost. However, computing the optimal transport plan requires solving a linear program over the target domain, whose complexity grows exponentially with the number of proposals K K . This is already costly for finite discrete state spaces and does not admit a tractable direct extension to continuous diffusion transitions. Computationally efficient approaches to list coupling have been studied in the context of language models; we provide a survey in the appendix. These methods, however, do not remain computationally tractable for continuous diffusion models. As a workaround, we draw inspiration from relative entropy coding (REC) ( Li, 2024 ; Flamich and Gündüz, 2026 ) , which is closely connected to speculative sampling, as elaborated below. REC is a class of algorithms that tackles a remote sampling problem: a sender, which has access to a target distribution ℚ \mathbb{Q} and a proposal distribution ℙ \mathbb{P} , communicates an index to a receiver, which shares ℙ \mathbb{P} , allowing the receiver to reproduce an exact sample from ℚ \mathbb{Q} . The fundamental communication cost of the index is governed, up to lower-order terms, by the relative entropy D KL ( ℚ ∥ ℙ ) D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb{Q}\|\mathbb{P}) , hence the name REC. Correspondingly, REC implementations, which can be based on Poisson processes ( Li and El Gamal, 2018 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) , dithered quantization ( Zamir and Feder, 1992 ) , or rejection sampling ( Harsha et al., 2010 ; Flamich and Theis, 2023 ; Flamich, 2023 ) , need to examine Ω ~ ( exp ( D KL ( ℚ ∥ ℙ ) ) ) \tilde{\Omega}(\exp(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb{Q}\|\mathbb{P}))) shared proposals before identifying the communicated sample. This viewpoint parallels speculative sampling: both problems seek to couple proposal samples with an exact target sample while maximizing the probability that the target can be recovered from the available proposals. While RMC optimizes the single-proposal overlap, measured by the total variation distance, REC algorithms construct exact couplings by processing an ordered sequence of proposal samples. Motivated by this connection, we replace the unrestricted list-coupling problem with an order-preserving sequence-coupling problem. In list coupling, the K K proposals may be jointly matched to the target without regard to their ordering; in sequence coupling, proposals are examined in their sampled order, and the first proposal satisfying the acceptance rule is selected.
